entries.title: We asked for your dream transit project. Here what you told us.
entries.summary: <p>We <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/10/09/nita-cta-metra-pace-budget-dream-project" target="_blank" >asked readers</a> last week to share dream projects they want the Northern Illinois Transit Agency to prioritize for the CTA, Metra and Pace in next year's budget.</p><p>Many of you asked for a dedicated north-south corridor to connect L lines outside of Downtown. The idea echoes the Circle Line concept, something the <a class="Link" href="https://www.transitchicago.com/loop-the-loop---proposal-for-new-circle-line/" target="_blank" >CTA proposed</a> in 2002. Gavin Rosenzweig has his own name for it.</p><p>"My dream project is the Outer Loop Connect," Rosenzweig told the Chicago Sun-Times. The plan would connect "via dedicated [bus rapid transit] or subway, all of the CTA and Metra branch stations along Western Avenue. This would allow a much easier transfer between spokes of the rail service lines."</p><p>Here's some of what dozens of you told us.</p><h3>New east-west connections</h3><p>"They need to start considering creating a Light Blue Line, stretching from the Lawrence Red Line stop, over the top of Lawrence Avenue, all the way to the Jefferson Park L stop on the Blue Line."<br>— Scott Benson</p><p>"Extend the Pink Line to Navy Pier. Extend the Brown Line further west to Jefferson Park."<br>— Mario Lupo</p><p>"As a North Side resident, I would like to see a more direct route to O’Hare. The fact I am parallel with the airport, but I need to go all the way downtown via the Red to pick up the Blue (or the proposed express train) is just a nonstarter for early morning flights. Either the Brown Line needs to be extended to connect to the Blue, or [bus rapid transit] on Western connects with the Blue."<br>— Nick Murphy</p><h3>Bus improvements</h3><p>"The No. 74 Fullerton bus should be extended east to Cannon Drive."<br>— Daniel Joseph, Evanston</p><p>"I would like NITA to expand seating options at bus stops and train stations and improve the design of existing bus shelters."<br>— PC Smith</p><h3>Metra</h3><p>"I would like to see more frequent Metra trains, especially on the weekends. The two-hour lead times are brutal."<br>— Kari Winge</p><p>"Electrification of Metra rail, modernization of stations, cleanliness and actual security and fare enforcement."<br>— Dominik Wojtysiak</p><p>"Connect Red Line Extension directly to the Metra Electric Line. There must be a direct same-station transfer here."<br>— Roger Deschner</p><h3>Safety and accessibility </h3><p>"Spend the money on making all stations ADA accessible. This is a no-brainer. Especially the Blue Line."<br>— Peggy Skorich</p><p>"Improve Pace paratransit reliability and service [with] flexible scheduling."<br>— Jasmine O.</p><p>"Put more Cook County Sheriffs on the buses and L train turnstiles to make sure people pay a full fare. Especially on the routes that run 24/7. (Especially at night)."<br>— Michael Sessions</p><p>"I want them to remove the police from buses in Black and Brown communities. It does not make us safer. It just makes riding public transit uncomfortable. And make transit free for riders who pay too much for buses and train fares."<br>— Charity Parker</p><p>"Major cities all over the world have one car per train reserved for women and children so riders don’t experience sexual harassment (Mexico City, Tokyo, etc.). This would cost nothing. In fact, it would make money by increasing ridership significantly."<br>— Noel Stringham</p><h3>And one very creative suggestion</h3><p>"Gondolas [like an enclosed ski lift] are edging into the realm of public transport. So how about running a gondola line between O'Hare and Union Station?"<br>— Scott Summers</p>

entries.title: 74th Columbus Day Parade led by Tony Danza
entries.summary: <p>The Joint Civic Committee of Italian Americans' 74th Columbus Day Parade kicked off Downtown Monday morning, days after the group and Cook County Treasurer Maria Pappas welcomed a special delegation from Italy during a flag-raising celebration.</p><p>Grand marshaled by actors Tony Danza and Cristiana Dell'Anna, as well as Lou Gramm, the original singer of the band Foreigner, the parade kicked off at 11:30 a.m. at Wacker Drive and Dearborn Street — forced from its traditional spot on State Street due to construction.</p><p>Among those marching in the parade were the Campagna Youth Orchestra, a 34-piece group from Campania, Italy, the parade's annual region of honor this year.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" entries.title: Video: Bears K Cairo Santos, Packers WR Matthew Golden appear to exchange cheap shots on punt return
entries.summary: <p>On a play almost certain to be reviewed by the NFL, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> kicker Cairo Santos appeared to stick his leg out in an attempt to trip Packers wide receiver Matthew Golden on a punt return in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/11/bears-coach-ben-johnson-runs-out-of-answers-unable-to-ignite-offense-in-31-7-loss-to-packers" >the Bears’ 31-7 loss at Lambeau Field</a> on Sunday.</p><p>A clip circulated by Fox after the game showed Golden running into the Bears’ sideline after his 17-yard punt return late in the first quarter. He bumped someone on the Bears staff and sent that person to the ground, then when he ran back toward the field, Santos kicked at his feet.</p><p>Here’s the video:</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">There's never any love lost between the Bears and Packers <a href="https://t.co/ohHDdIXX8e">pic.twitter.com/ohHDdIXX8e</a></p>— FOX Sports: NFL (@NFLonFOX) <a href="https://x.com/NFLonFOX/status/2109386901371437458?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">October 11, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Neither player has commented on the play, but in both cases, it appeared to be avoidable.</p><p>Santos had a rough game, missing his only field goal, a 43-yarder early in the third quarter with the Bears down 20-7, while Golden finished with six catches for 123 yards and returned two punts for a total of 27 yards.</p><p>The game was a mess overall for the Bears, who went into Green Bay as favorites, but fell behind 14-0 early and never recovered as they suffered their worst loss since Week 2 of last season.</p>

entries.title: Root out abuse built on white supremacy, religious intolerance.
entries.summary: <p>Months after a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer shot and <a class="Link" href="https://mainebeacon.com/ice-killed-johan-duran-guerrero-his-family-is-still-waiting-for-answers-justice/" target="_blank" >killed</a> Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Biddeford, Maine, no one has been charged.</p><p>He was 25. He was Colombian. He had a 3-year-old daughter. He had a federal work permit.</p><p>Homeland Security says its officer feared for public safety. Sen. Angus King's, I-Maine, office says Durán Guerrero was not the operation's target. The agency acknowledges granting him that permit last year.</p><p>A fear, a wrong man and a work permit. One dead man, no charges. The agents didn't wear body cameras.</p><p>It may surprise people today, but from the first colonies right through this year's ICE operations, this country has treated immigrants from Catholic countries as expendable. Of every color.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-ad0000" name="module-ad0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>In 1891, a mob stormed the parish prison in New Orleans and killed 11 Italians and Italian Americans. <a class="Link" href="https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1891/d634" target="_blank" >Emmanuele Polizzi</a> was dragged outside, hanged from a lamppost and shot as he hung there. Some were citizens. A grand jury refused to indict anyone.</p><p>Nobody answered for those 11 men, because nobody with power was made to look.</p><p>When the Ku Klux Klan was refounded in 1915, it joined its war on Black freedom to a campaign against Catholic immigrants and their American-born children. Being white was not enough. Catholics were accused of owing allegiance to a foreign pope. The Klan targeted their churches and the schools their children attended.</p><p>Maine became a Klan stronghold, and the people it went after were French Canadian Catholics. Nobody today would hesitate to call them white.</p><p>My father was born in Biddeford. My father is white.</p><p>On Labor Day in 1924, about 300 Klansmen marched through neighboring Saco. Biddeford's mayor, Edward Drapeau, the son of Canadian immigrants, warned them to remain in Saco "at all times thereafter." He ordered police to guard the bridges.</p><p>The Klan did not cross.</p><p>Biddeford's mayor today keeps that newspaper page in his office. He pulled it out again in July.</p><p>The Catholics the Klan hunted did something else. The Knights of Columbus named themselves for a Catholic explorer America had made a hero. Then they commissioned W.E.B. Du Bois to write a history of Black Americans' contributions, to answer what their historical commission called "the wave of racial and religious ostracism" sweeping the country. "The Gift of Black Folk" appeared in 1924.</p><p>The Klan was coming for them. They spent their money making somebody else's case.</p><p>In 2009, during my tenure leading the NAACP, the Knights put that book back into print for the association's 100th anniversary.</p><p>Len Riggio chose the same way. Len was a friend. I once asked the man who built Barnes & Noble into a national chain why he cared about racial justice.</p><p>"Because I'm old enough to remember when my people were lynched too."</p><p>Len was Italian American, born in Little Italy. He supported the NAACP in New York. He and his wife, Louise, funded a chapel at the Children's Defense Fund's Tennessee farm. It carries his name and Bill Lynch's, the Black organizer who became New York's deputy mayor and served on that board beside him. Both men are gone. Their names remain together.</p><p>My father's grandfather chose another way. A Protestant of northern English stock, himself the grandson of immigrants, he disinherited my father for marrying my mother, who is Black. My father's mother and brothers refused to go along.</p><p>A family can produce a bigot and still refuse to follow him.</p><p>In 2011, Paul LePage, raised in a French Canadian Catholic family in Lewiston, told the NAACP to "kiss my butt." I was the association's president. I reminded him that he owed his own chance to people who stood up to the Klan in his state.</p><p>This September he said a member of his own family faced deportation despite holding a work permit. "That's not right," he said.</p><p>I am glad he said it. But ICE arrested 488 people in Maine through July, more than in 2024 and 2025 combined, according to federal data, and one analysis found nearly 90% had no criminal conviction.</p><p>LePage has learned the wrong lesson if concern stops at his own family. The family down the street deserves the same.</p><p>Thirty-nine senators demanded answers from Homeland Security in July. House Democrats held an unofficial hearing in Biddeford in August, because the majority would not call a real one, and even they could not get ICE to confirm whom its agents were looking for.</p><p>Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, chairs the Senate Appropriations Committee, which writes Homeland Security's budget. She was not among the 39 who signed. It is time for her to demand that the administration account for how a hardworking father with a work permit was shot dead on a Biddeford street despite not being the target of the operation, and that every report, every radio log, every witness statement go to Maine's attorney general.</p><h3>Stamp out intolerance</h3><p>No U.S. senator should have to think twice about asking that question.</p><p>Congress should also put body cameras and visible identification into law. That is how a country finds out what happened. It is what nobody did in 1891.</p><p>Most Americans understand we need to move past our nation's patterns of racism and antisemitism. As we do, let us widen the coalition to root out every pattern of abuse built on white supremacy and religious intolerance.</p><p>Ask your children how your family became American. Tell them who opened the door. Tell them who tried to close it.</p><p>We came here in different boats. We are in the same boat now. It only stays afloat if we keep one another from sinking.</p><p><i>Ben Jealous is a professor of practice at the University of Pennsylvania and former president and CEO of the NAACP.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-ae0000" name="module-ae0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Concert will help underserved community tune into energy careers
entries.summary: <p>America's energy sector is growing rapidly, driven by infrastructure investment, technological innovation and the transition to a more modern energy economy. Yet one question remains: Will the communities too often left behind be part of that growth?</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://nul.org/news/state-black-america-call-crisis-charge?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=22842484274&gbraid=0AAAAADmWGJEToTO1Jo7EEsxHGpK1fjpH9&gclid=CjwKCAjwirLWBhBBEiwAlItbEt723Fn9E6xmxHGm9sAM6BsAZIDu-690wwG3AF4ekgY8XedJveDj8xoCULgQAvD_BwE" target="_blank" >National Urban League</a> believes they must be.</p><p>That is why we are partnering with the <a class="Link" href="https://chiul.org/" target="_blank" >Chicago Urban League</a> and the <a class="Link" href="https://cewd.org/" target="_blank" >Center for Energy Workforce Development</a> — with philanthropic support from <a class="Link" href="https://investinourfuture.org/" target="_blank" >Invest in Our Future</a> — on "Energy Up Chicago," a free workforce engagement and concert experience Wednesday at the House of Blues, 329 N. Dearborn St.</p><p>It may look like a free concert with headliner BabyChiefDoIt, guests Star Bandz and Mother Nature, and DJ sets from Power 92's DJ Pharris and DJ Nephets. But in reality, it is a workforce development strategy.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-e50000" name="module-e50000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>Energy Up Chicago is built on a simple idea: If we want young adults to explore career opportunities, we have to meet them where they are. By combining music, mentorship, employer engagement and career exploration, we are introducing participants to an industry they may never have considered, but one that offers some of the most promising pathways to economic mobility in America today.</p><p>The event is part of the the <a class="Link" href="https://nul.org/program/urban-energy-jobs-program" target="_blank" >Energy Jobs Program</a>, a partnership between the Urban League and Center for Energy Workforce Development, created to diversify the energy workforce and expand access to high-quality careers. The program connects energy companies with Urban League affiliates, which recruit and prepare candidates through community-based training, mentorship and workforce readiness programs.</p><p>The results speak for themselves.</p><p>Over the last four years, the Urban Energy Jobs Program has placed nearly 500 people into energy careers across Chicago, Houston, Louisville, New Orleans and St. Louis. Those placements have generated more than $20 million in economic mobility, with participants earning an average starting wage of $21 per hour.</p><p>These are not temporary jobs. They are careers with opportunities for advancement, stability and family-sustaining wages.</p><p>That opportunity is especially important in Chicago. Illinois' energy sector employs roughly 5% percent of the state's workforce, yet many residents remain unaware of the industry's breadth. Energy careers extend far beyond power generation. They include construction, manufacturing, engineering, cybersecurity, information technology, skilled trades, environmental services and business operations. Many of these careers can be accessed through apprenticeships, certifications and technical training rather than a four-year degree.</p><p>Energy careers also extend beyond traditional utilities. They include building trades; workers constructing solar farms; manufacturing workers fabricating batteries and turbines; and engineers keeping our grid resilient and responsive by planning for known and unknown changes in supply and demand.</p><p>For too long, Black communities and other underserved populations have faced barriers to entering fast-growing industries. Closing those gaps requires more than good intentions. It requires partnerships that connect talent with opportunity.</p><p>That is exactly what the Urban Energy Jobs Program was designed to do.</p><p>The Center for Energy Workforce Development and the National Urban League launched the initiative because the energy industry needs a workforce that better reflects the communities it serves. The goal is to make careers in energy as attractive, accessible and widely understood as careers in technology, medicine or law, while creating clear pathways into the workforce for people who may never have seen energy as a viable option.</p><p>The Chicago Urban League plays a critical role in that effort. Its deep community relationships and workforce expertise help ensure residents are not simply informed about opportunities but are prepared to pursue them.</p><p>At a time when employers across the energy sector are searching for skilled workers, expanding access to these careers is both an economic imperative and an equity imperative. The nation cannot afford to overlook talent that exists in every neighborhood and every community.</p><p>Workforce development is often discussed in abstract terms. Energy Up Chicago makes it tangible.</p><p>When a young person walks into the House of Blues and leaves with a connection to an employer, an apprenticeship opportunity, or a roadmap to a career, that is more than workforce development. It is economic mobility in action.</p><p>The future of the energy industry will depend on who gets access to the opportunities it creates. Our goal is simple: to ensure that opportunity reaches everyone.</p><p>While Wednesday's event is at capacity, people can sign up on the standby waitlist at<a class="Link" href="https://makeanimpactconcerts.org/chicago" target="_blank" > makeanimpactconcerts.org/chicago</a>.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/authors/marc-h-morial" target="_blank" ><i>Marc H. Morial</i></a><i> is president and CEO of the National Urban League</i> <i>and</i> <i>was mayor of New Orleans from 1994 to 2002.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-890000" name="module-890000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Student eager to move despite mental health struggles
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I'm 34 years old and have been diagnosed with schizoaffective bipolar disorder. I have been in treatment for years with a psychiatrist and a therapist, and I take my medication daily as instructed. I do not drink or use drugs. I am committed to my mental health to prove that people like me can lead full lives.</p><p>My family wants me to stay where they live forever, but I dream of moving back down south, where I lived on my own before. I loved the culture, art, weather and friends. Whenever I bring it up, they dismiss it. I think they're afraid that I will start hallucinating again and not have a support system there.</p><p>I will be graduating soon from a master's program in counseling, and I look at jobs online all the time. Is it wise to move away from my family with my disorder? Do I sit them down and explain that I was my happiest when I lived there and want to return? I love them and don't want to hurt them. I think if I have a plan in place and stay on track with medication, it would be safe. — <i>CONFLICTED IN THE NORTH</i></p><p><b>DEAR CONFLICTED:</b> Have you discussed this with your therapist and psychiatrist? If they both sign off on the move, your family will have less cause for concern. Bring a family spokesperson with you and have your therapist go over the support plan for your new environment. The spokesperson can then help you ease the worries of the rest of the family.</p><p>If, however, your care providers don't think it's wise to move right now, please listen to them. Ask them to outline some milestones you can work toward to make moving south a healthier goal for the future.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My brother died a year ago. I have been visiting his widow, "Cheryl," twice a month ever since. She lives an hour away and doesn't get around very well. I drive to her house, and I treasure my time with her. She was the love of my brother's life.</p><p>My problem is my sister, "Kate." Kate is self-centered, whiny, disruptive and generally unpleasant. I spend as little time as possible with her. I know that as soon as she finds out about them, Kate will expect to be included in my visits with Cheryl. I haven't mentioned them, as I would rather not include her. What I would like to see happen is for Kate to come up with her own plan to visit with Cheryl. I love Kate and don't want to hurt her, but on the other hand, I don't want her to ruin my visits with Cheryl either. What should I do? — <i>BAD SISTER IN MISSOURI</i></p><p><b>DEAR SISTER:</b> There's no reason for you to hurt your sister's feelings. Tell Kate you feel one-on-one visits with your brother's grieving widow are more beneficial than overwhelming her with additional company. Then (with Cheryl's permission) suggest that Kate call Cheryl and make some plans to visit with her on her own. If Kate argues, see if you can get Cheryl to back you up.</p><p>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</p>

entries.title: Gubernatorial grudge match pits Gov. JB Pritzker against Darren Bailey
entries.summary: <p>Illinois voters have gotten to know incumbent Democratic Gov. JB Pritzker through the darkest days of a pandemic, bouts of civil unrest and repeated clashes with President Donald Trump’s administration.</p><p>During a volatile decade for the state, voters have also grown familiar with Pritzker’s most frequent state-level foil: Darren Bailey, the fiery Republican farmer and former downstate legislator who’s trying to keep the focus on Illinois’ economic, education and public safety issues — and off his longtime support of Trump.</p><p>Next month’s general election grudge match pits a progressive governor downplaying his potential White House ambitions as he seeks a rare third term, against the hardline conservative who has taken up residence in the city he famously branded a “<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2022/9/13/23351525/hellhole-republican-darren-bailey-chicago-john-hancock-center-north-side-downstate-pritzker-governor" target="_blank" ><u>hellhole</u></a>” before <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/11/8/23448412/j-b-pritzker-declares-victory-over-gop-challenger-darren-bailey" >getting thumped by Pritzker four years ago.</a></p><p>Aiming for the role of conversation starter if not spoiler in the Illinois governor race is independent candidate Collin Corbett, a moderate millennial Republican strategist who defected from his party because he thinks there’s middle ground to be found between Pritzker and Bailey in the acutely polarized politics of 2026.</p><h3><b>Pritzker back ‘on the reins’</b></h3><p>Pritzker, 61, started checking a host of boxes on an ambitious legislative agenda soon after unseating Republican former Gov. Bruce Rauner and taking office in 2019, shepherding the legalization of recreational marijuana and raising the state’s minimum wage to $15 per hour.</p><p>The billionaire former entrepreneur and philanthropist also championed a $45 billion capital infrastructure upgrade plan, funded largely by the legalization of sports betting and expanding Illinois’ vast array of gambling options, including the introduction of a Chicago casino (Pritzker himself is a prolific poker and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/illinois-governor/2025/10/16/jb-pritzker-gambling-blackjack-win-las-vegas" target="_blank" ><u>blackjack player</u></a> who used to have a stake in Elgin’s Grand Victoria Casino).</p><p>A fixture on TV screens statewide with daily updates in the depths of the COVID-19 pandemic, Pritzker drew complaints from many business owners who said his closures lasted too long, but public health experts noted the state suffered fewer deaths on average compared to those that took a more lax approach.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div </div> </div><p>Cruising to reelection by nearly 13 percentage points over Bailey in 2022, Pritzker went on to sign Illinois’ assault weapons ban and a series of laws bolstering the state’s’ status as a haven for abortion care, while the cash-strapped state has seen 12 credit rating upgrades from the near-junk status he inherited.</p><p>“Things were heading in the wrong direction in 2018 literally in every way you can imagine,” Pritzker told the Sun-Times. “We had to change the direction of the state.”</p><p>The Hyatt hotel heir with an estimated net worth of $4.2 billion dropped $65 million into his gubernatorial campaign <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/08/17/gov-jb-pritzker-pours-65m-into-his-campaign-fund-ahead-of-november-elections" target="_blank" ><u>this summer</u></a>, pushing his personal tab over three campaigns past $400 million.</p><p>That’s not counting millions more that Pritzker has directed to fellow Democrats and left-leaning causes across the nation and at home, including $58 million he pumped into his most notable state-level loss: the failed 2020 effort to amend Illinois’ constitution allowing for a graduated state income tax.</p><p>This time around, Pritzker’s team is blanketing airwaves and the internet with ads reminding voters of Bailey’s strong support for Trump, his staunch opposition to abortion rights and his rejection of science that shows dinosaurs never coexisted with humans, as taught in curriculum at <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/08/20/darren-bailey-illinois-republicans-state-fair-pritzker" target="_blank" ><u>a Bailey-founded school</u></a>.</p><p>“He's ashamed of the positions that he's had in the past, and he hopes that the voters won't hold it against him, but we know he hasn't changed,” Pritzker said.</p><p>“The difference between JB Pritzker in 2019 and JB Pritzker in 2026 is that I come into the next four years as governor as somebody who has his hands fully on the reins of the state, and is able to maneuver it in a way that I think is highly beneficial for our future.”</p><h3><b>‘Completely different attitude’ for Bailey</b></h3><p>Bailey’s campaign has presented a softer candidate compared to the one who unleashed a flamethrower on a supposed copy of the state budget in a 2022 ad.</p><p>This time, the farmer and former state senator from Xenia in southern Illinois is hammering many of the same themes as Democrats are nationwide: affordability, education and public safety.</p><p>But Bailey, 60, knows his biggest hurdle is making inroads with voters in Chicago area precincts where Pritzker racked up double-digit margins four years ago. Bailey moved into a South Loop apartment in April, not far from the downtown condo he rented during his ill-fated introduction to city voters in 2022.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-030000" name="image-030000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3ca18ac/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1024x575+0+53/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff2%2Ff7%2Ff7457b2a3b0018e5cd7d77854d98%2Fbailey.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d8a5b5b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1024x575+0+53/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff2%2Ff7%2Ff7457b2a3b0018e5cd7d77854d98%2Fbailey.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f3d5257/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1024x575+0+53/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff2%2Ff7%2Ff7457b2a3b0018e5cd7d77854d98%2Fbailey.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Republican gubernatorial candidate Darren Bailey, shown here posing with a supporter in Elmhurst in 2023. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f3d5257/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1024x575+0+53/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff2%2Ff7%2Ff7457b2a3b0018e5cd7d77854d98%2Fbailey.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6dee939/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1024x575+0+53/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff2%2Ff7%2Ff7457b2a3b0018e5cd7d77854d98%2Fbailey.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f3d5257/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1024x575+0+53/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff2%2Ff7%2Ff7457b2a3b0018e5cd7d77854d98%2Fbailey.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Republican gubernatorial candidate Darren Bailey, shown here posing with a supporter in Elmhurst in 2023. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“There's more people that live in the apartment unit that [wife] Cindy and I stay in than in my hometown,” he said. “I'm seeing and meeting new faces every day, up and down the elevator.”</p><p>Those interactions indicate to Bailey that “It is a completely different attitude and atmosphere than it was four years ago,” he said.</p><p>“I don't think Chicago and this area — I don't think they were feeling the failures of the SAFE-T Act. I don't think they were feeling the financial burden four years ago. They're feeling all of that right now,” said Bailey, who grew his political profile as a staunch opponent of Pritzker’s COVID-19 mitigations and masking mandates.</p><p>Complicating matters for Bailey is the fact that suburban voters who used to provide the lifeblood of the Illinois GOP have mostly rejected Trump. The president rallied alongside Bailey in 2022 and urged him to stay in the governor race following the deaths of Bailey’s son, daughter-in-law and two grandchildren in a helicopter crash last fall.</p><p>Trump has given <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/09/14/trump-endorses-bailey-pritzker-illinois-governor-race" target="_blank" ><u>another endorsement to Bailey</u></a>, who has said he appreciates the White House support but quickly shifted the focus back to “the endless ways JB Pritzker has failed Illinois families over the last eight years.”</p><p>Bailey’s campaign has gone out of its way to flag his divergence from Trump on certain instances, including Bailey’s opposition to data centers that the president has said should be welcomed by local governments.</p><p>He entered July with about $128,000 in his campaign fund and has raised almost $300,000 since then, as megadonors have slowed investments in a state that has gone more than a decade without a Republican winning a statewide contest.</p><p>“I'm not standing here and touting the Republican Party,” Bailey said. “We have problems. Everything is broken in Illinois, and it needs to get fixed. But it needs a leader who will stand up and listen to everybody.”</p><h3><b>Independent shocker?</b></h3><p>Dissatisfied with the prospect of another Bailey campaign “telling people what they want to entries.title: V.V. Lightbody celebrates new album with two show at the Hideout in Chicago
entries.summary: <p>V.V. Lightbody wants to assure everybody that there were no flutes harmed in the making of her new<a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RUJbuhAxs00" target="_blank" ><u>“Practice Smiling” music video.</u></a></p><p>“It was a broken flute; it was ready to be destroyed,” the singer joked during a recent conversation at the WBEZ studios. In the video, Lightbody toys with new ways to use the instrument: It’s a hair curler, a hand weight, a telescope. At one point, she swims in Lake Michigan while pursing her lips to the mouth holes and then dunks it underwater just for the hell of it. “It felt really fun to put the flute into new settings,” she said.</p><p>Thankfully she had some backups. For more than a decade, Lightbody has become known as “the flute lady” about town. “I was ahead of the curve though,” she joked, taking aim at the theory that Lizzo was the only one to make the flute cool again.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-ba0000" name="module-ba0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>V.V. Lightbody</h3><br><b>When:</b> 7 p.m. Oct. 15-16<br><b>Where:</b> Hideout, 1354 W. Wabansia Ave.<br><b>Tickets:</b> $26<br><b>Info:</b> hideoutchicago.com</div> </div><p>In Chicago, Lightbody (whose real name is Vivian McConnell) is permanently on the indie rock speed dial, called upon any time a band gets a craving for some extra wind instruments. She’s worked with Twin Peaks, Whitney, Finom and Elizabeth Moen. And demand is not just among Chicago musicians — let’s not forget Harry Styles.</p><p>“That was a crazy one-off scenario,” she said of filling in for his gig at the BBC Radio One's Big Weekend Festival in 2022, also contributing keys, guitar and vocals, all of which she is equally versed in. “A friend was working with his musical director and they needed a last-minute player. They knew that I could do it and would show up and wouldn't be weird,” she said. Though the placement didn’t shoot her up the charts, “It definitely helped people be like, OK, Viv is still doing this and she's not going away, which was really powerful.” </p><p>But after years of supporting other musicians, including being a proud “album doula” in the studio, Lightbody is finally back with her first proper solo album in six years and will celebrate with two shows at Hideout Oct. 15 and 16. Cheekily called “Period Piece,” and released on Oct. 9 via Egghunt Records, it’s fully self-produced and comes with many meanings. It could be about menstruation (there’s also a song called “There Will Be Blood”). It definitely marks the end of one figurative sentence and the beginning of a new one in her career. But she also just really loved watching period piece films and shows when she was making the record.</p><p> “I was loving all the Jane Austen stuff, I would watch every version of ‘Sense and Sensibility.’ And ‘Gilded Age’ and ‘The Empress,’” she said. “I was maybe a little depressed and just feeling like escaping and found myself being almost obsessed with what these women were doing and why do their lives feel so simple and easy … even though they weren’t.” </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a And demand is not just among Chicago musicians — let’s not forget Harry Styles.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Now 36, Lightbody was also wrapped up in her own womanhood, thinking about aging and going through a new transition in her life. “The album is definitely woven with anxiety and feelings and big emotions,” she said of the 10 tracks that swim with her eclectic jazz, rock and Brazilian music influences and reciprocal contributions from friends and collaborators like Macie Stewart, Sam Cantor, Emma Hospelhorn, Jack Henry Lickerman and Cassandra Jenkins.</p><p>“Practice Smiling,” for example, was about the overwhelming sense of social anxiety she felt after the pandemic and remembering the first show she went to after the lockdown, to see her friend Sima Cunningham at Constellation. “I was dancing all night. And then I took my sweater off and threw out my back,” she joked. “I was like, oh my God, I've been holding on to a lot of tension. And I've aged since I've seen everybody.”</p><p>Later, she dissects her flight anxiety on the soft-spoken “Patience Like a Pilot” and ponders what happens if people start falling in love with artificial intelligence on “Robocaller.” She also wonders if we’re all just caught up in constantly looking for meaning in arbitrary signs on “Two Swans,” though she got a dose of it herself when, six days after she released the song in mid-September, Lincoln Park Zoo got a pair of its own with new avian inhabitants Dean and Dolly. “Now I’ve been texting everybody, like does anybody know anybody who works there?” the singer joked, thinking about ways for local cross-collabs.</p><p>Lightbody has in fact had a long thing of seeing two swans. It started when she was a kid growing up in Dixon, Illinois, where her neighbors actually had a pair as pets, “and then I just started seeing them everywhere.” The most recent example was when she moved into a new apartment in Hermosa and found the shower doors etched with the birds. “I knew I was in the right place,” she said. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-3d0000" name="image-3d0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/708587f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6830x3833+0+815/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffa%2F22%2F8cc6869b464188ddc9fac876f61e%2Fvvlightbody-261015-011.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/bd5ac10/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6830x3833+0+815/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffa%2F22%2F8cc6869b464188ddc9fac876f61e%2Fvvlightbody-261015-011.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/cdd02f1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6830x3833+0+815/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffa%2F22%2F8cc6869b464188ddc9fac876f61e%2Fvvlightbody-261015-011.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Musician V.V. But on “Period Piece,” she goes back to her farm-town family roots and conjures a special period in her ancestors’ life, too. Lightbody ends the “Patience Like A Pilot” track with recordings of her great-grandfather Randall Lightbody’s big band, the Blossom Heath Entertainers, who used to travel through Chicago for gigs. Her grandmother, Virginia Lightbody, was also a piano player. And V.V. has honored that legacy by adopting the surname as her nom de plume.</p><p>But if she’s learned anything from that time period when they lived and worked as musicians, it’s perhaps to slow down a little. “It feels so cliche to say but everybody needs to be reminded of that, especially now with technology and everything, it's easy to feel really overwhelmed,” said Lightbody. “In these songs, I’m thinking deeply and feeling the world pretty heavily … you feel the pressure of a person who's trying to live, but that feels really exciting to me.”</p>

entries.title: Long a foregone conclusion, property tax hikes will no longer be a given under elected CPS board
entries.summary: <p>Chicago’s school board has long relied on increasing property taxes annually — the only avenue the school district has available to raise revenue on its own. Those increases have generated more than $100 million every year and helped balance the underfunded school district’s budget.</p><p>But with the Chicago Public Schools board moving from mayoral control to the entire school board being elected for the first time on Nov. 3, new political considerations mean tax hikes might no longer be a foregone conclusion.</p><p>More than two-thirds of the 45 candidates for 21 seats on the new board said in a WBEZ/Chicago Sun-Times questionnaire that they would not vote to raise property taxes to the limit if elected — including two of the three people vying to be school board president.</p><p>For candidates hoping to win votes, the decision might seem like a no-brainer, given that many Chicago residents already feel overwhelmed by property taxes.</p><p>But forgoing that tax revenue won’t be easy. Coming into this school year, CPS faced a $730 million deficit. If it hadn’t raised property taxes to the limit, the hole would have been almost $900 million.</p><p>CPS is grappling with rising costs, like other government bodies, and has aging buildings in need of critical repairs. It’s also serving students with more needs. As a result, CPS employs 5,500 more special education teachers and aides than it did seven years ago.</p><p>“The board as a whole is really going to be put between a rock and a hard place in regards to property tax revenue,” said Arnie Rivera, who previously served as CPS chief operating officer and a board member. “I get why they don't want to continue the reliance on property taxes. With that being said, the district is in a difficult financial situation where its expenses are grossly outpacing its revenues.”</p><p>And avoiding raising property taxes has consequences for future years.</p><p>“If [CPS] skips doing that increase this year, it can't go back next year and add that on,” said Danny Vesecky, senior policy and research associate at the Civic Federation, a fiscal watchdog group. “So if CPS skips increasing its levy this year, that doesn't just mean it loses $100 million this year. It means it loses that money every year going forward.”</p><p>If the board didn’t increase property taxes for any of the past five years, the district’s property tax levy would be about $500 million less.</p><p>CPS receives the largest share of property taxes collected — about half of each taxpayer's bill. And the amount CPS draws from property taxes has doubled over the past two decades. That’s due in part to special assessments put in place by former Mayor Rahm Emanuel. The school board has the power to boost the property tax levy up to inflation or by 5% — whichever is less — and to account for new or re-assessed property.</p><p>Hilario Dominguez is the only school board presidential candidate who has said he will continue to raise property taxes to the limit until more state education funding is secured.</p><p>“I'll say that anyone up here that tells you they're not going to levy the property taxes — the only thing that CPS can do — is either lying or they don't understand the responsibility of this job,” Dominguez said.</p><p>Without that additional revenue, Dominguez, who is endorsed by the Chicago Teachers Union, said the school board will have to move forward with “cuts and closures and less for our students.”</p><p>Jessica Biggs, a current school board member and candidate for board president, voted to increase property taxes every time the question was put in front of her the past two years.</p><p>But Biggs said she would not turn to property tax increases as board president because they are regressive, requiring “more from those who are least capable of paying.”</p><p>Biggs, who is endorsed by the union representing CPS support staff, said she would try to balance the district’s budget by reducing administrative costs. She also laid out a plan to try to get the state to provide more money for CPS with a focus on having the state cover teacher pension costs, as it does for other school districts.</p><p>CPS has already trimmed significantly over the past two years to reduce deficits, and officials have said they don’t think there’s much more to cut. A budget director declared last year that all the “low hanging fruit” has been picked.</p><p>As for the pensions, Emanuel convinced the state to allow the city to collect a special levy to be used only for teacher pensions. If the state were to pick up the cost for pensions, it is unclear what would happen to that levy, Vesecky said. It could turn out that property tax bills decrease but CPS sees no financial benefit.</p><p>Rivera said state lawmakers might frown upon a decision by the board not to increase property taxes to the limit.</p><p>“The state of Illinois is going to feel as though, ‘Hey, CPS, you're coming to us asking us for more revenue, but you're not maximizing the revenue that you directly control.’”</p><p>Victor Henderson, the third candidate for board president and a prominent defense attorney who is not endorsed by any unions, said he does not think increasing property taxes should be automatic. He also won’t immediately go to the state for more funding. As an outsider, he said he thinks the district’s $10 billion budget should be enough to cover expenses and wants a forensic audit completed.</p><p>“We shouldn't ask you to pay another dime before we know that each and every dime that's being spent is being spent properly,” he said. “Then we figure out what to do.”</p>

entries.title: Chicago Bears edition of Hallmark’s ‘Holiday Touchdown’ is a gooey homage to the city
entries.summary: <p>Talk about a Sweet Home Chicago.</p><p>“Holiday Touchdown: A Bears Love Story” is like a game plan where the coaches write down the first 15 offensive snaps in advance, and the team follows that script to the letter. It’s a predictable, time-tested, winning formula, with few surprises and a high degree of safety.</p><p>Filmed during the blistering heat of July (kudos to the actors and extras wearing their winter layers), this third entry in the “Holiday Touchdown” franchise (after Kansas City and Buffalo) brings the Hallmark recipe to Chicago. Look, we know this material isn’t going to have the profanity and scorched-earth emotional content of something like “The Bear” or “The Chi.”</p><p>With solid direction from Dustin Rikert, this is a warm-hearted, eggnog-laced version of Chicago during the holidays, where it’s all about the open-air holiday market, singing Christmas karaoke, getting together with family — and rooting for the Bears to beat those Packers. As such, it’s a lovely slice of comfort viewing, with excellent production values, fine work by the talented cast, and exactly the kind of ending we’ve come to expect and appreciate from the team at Hallmark. (Disclosure: My sister, Laura Roeper, was the prop master for this film.)</p><p>“Holiday Touchdown: A Bears Love Story” kicks off with a prologue set at Soldier Field on December 19, 1971. With archival footage of Dick Butkus and Bobby Douglass as the backdrop, a young woman named Darlene (Heidi Musec) meets up with a young fella named Bernie (Nathan Adams Stark) for their first date. They fall in love — and fall in love with going to Bears games.</p><p>Cut to present day, with “This Christmas” by Donny Hathaway on the soundtrack, and we’re at the Irish Nobleman Pub in West Town. The Bears game is on the TVs, but that doesn’t mean much to the New York-based freelance reporter Avery Clark (Lyndsy Fonseca), who is in town to visit her mother, Jody (Barbara Alyn Woods), and her stepfather, Ron (Khary Payton), who run the bar.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" entries.title: UChicago frat suspends events after report of sexual assault; students question campus training, Greek life
entries.summary: <p>After a woman reported being sexually assaulted at a University of Chicago fraternity house, some students are calling for accountability and questioning the effectiveness of the university's sexual assault prevention and training efforts.</p><p>The 21-year-old woman told police she was sexually assaulted early Sunday at the Alpha Epsilon Pi fraternity, according to Chicago police and a university community alert. The woman told officers the assault occurred around 1:50 a.m. at the fraternity house, 5625 S. University Ave., and was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center for treatment.</p><p>According to The Chicago Maroon, the student newspaper, <a class="Link" href="https://chicagomaroon.com/53960/news/sexual-assault-reported-at-aepi-fraternity-house/" target="_blank" >the assault occurred during a party</a>.</p><p>Area 1 detectives are investigating.</p><p>The report comes amid renewed national attention on sexual violence in Greek life following a case at Cornell University. In September, a former Cornell student filed a lawsuit alleging that seven men raped her at a Chi Phi fraternity house in 2024. The case has prompted student protests and walkouts across the country in solidarity — including a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/10/08/lincoln-park-high-students-walk-out-jane-doe-cornell-rape-case" target="_blank" >walkout at Lincoln Park High School in Chicago</a> last week. </p><p>Zuzanna Wolodko, a fourth-year University of Chicago doctoral student from Poland, said she was struck by how soon the reported assault occurred after the Cornell case.</p><p>“It kind of surprised me that literally within two weeks someone would do the same thing,” Wolodko said. It was the first time in her four years on campus that she recalled receiving a university email about a sexual assault, she added.</p><p>Wolodko said graduate students complete annual online training that covers sexual assault and how to help someone who's been assaulted. But she questioned whether the format was effective and said, as a teaching assistant, she wanted more concrete guidance on supporting undergraduate students.</p><p>In addition to the Chicago Police Department's criminal investigation, the university is gathering information and would initiate disciplinary proceedings when possible, a UChicago spokesperson said.</p><p>The university "remains committed to addressing sexual misconduct cases that occur, to imposing disciplinary consequences as warranted, and to continually improving efforts to prevent sexual misconduct," the university wrote She said she wasn't surprised that an assault occurred. </p><p>“I think it's just kind of par for the course, unfortunately, on any college campus,” she said, describing how stories of sexual violence sometimes circulate among students, even if they aren’t officially reported.</p><p>Flores says Greek life can be patriarchal and reinforce traditional gender roles, often doing more harm than good. She said she hopes the student responsible would be expelled and not offered any alternative — and less harsh — punishment. </p><p>Yuliia Ihnatesku, a 2026 UChicago graduate visiting campus on Monday, said students often drive campus conversations about sexual violence. Both Flores and Ihnatesku said they had not noticed any additional university communication or programming following the Cornell case.</p><p>In a statement to the Sun-Times, AEPi's national headquarters said it learned of the UChicago incident Sunday afternoon and had been working with Lambda Chapter leadership since then. The chapter was told not to hold events or programs while the investigation is pending.</p><p>The organization said all AEPi members receive mandatory training on its standards against sexual harassment and assault, and that violations may lead to expulsion.</p><p>“While this inquiry is at its outset, we will refrain from jumping to any conclusion until the investigation is complete,” the statement said.</p><p>Sophomore Andrew Zheng, a transfer student who started at UChicago three weeks ago, said he was disappointed to hear about the reported assault. He called for an investigation involving AEPi and said people should recognize that “one little event in their night can ruin someone else's life.”</p><p>“I thought UChicago, being such an upstanding institution about a lot of things, I'd expect a lot better,” Zheng said.</p>
